recipe.history:
The double patty burger is, in many ways, the purest expression of what America did with the hamburger once it claimed it as its own. The hamburger itself arrived in American consciousness through German immigration in the late nineteenth century — the 'Hamburg steak,' a dish of minced or ground beef patted into a round and cooked, was a familiar offering at German immigrant restaurants in New York and at food stalls at the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair, where the sandwich form — ground beef between bread — was popularized for the masses. The double patty was a natural evolution driven by the American appetite for abundance and the engineering logic of fast-food systems: two thinner patties cook faster than one thick one, cover more bread surface area, and allow for a more even cheese-to-meat ratio. The double cheeseburger became the default expression of seriousness in American burger culture — from the Double-Double at In-N-Out Burger, conceived in 1963, to the Big Mac's twin patties, to the countless smash burger variations that dominate the burger conversation today. Aged cheddar on a double patty burger is the adult upgrade on the processed American cheese of the classic drive-through: the same concept — a sharp, melted, orange-golden layer between the patties — but with the mineral complexity and long-cave depth of a properly aged cheese standing in for its more democratic predecessor.

Bacon's role in American cuisine is so thoroughly established as to be almost invisible as history — it simply seems as though bacon has always been there, on every diner menu, in every BLT, on every burger that aspires to seriousness. But the bacon cheeseburger as a specific, codified American configuration has a traceable history: it emerged as a menu item in the 1940s and 1950s in roadside diners and drive-ins, and became national shorthand for indulgence and satisfaction in a way that few other food combinations have managed to replicate. The special sauce — a thousand-island-adjacent, mayo-and-pickle-relish-based condiment — was popularized by McDonald's Big Mac in 1968 and has since spawned a thousand variations, each restaurant asserting its own claim to the ideal balance of creamy, tangy, sweet, and savory. A brioche bun, iceberg lettuce, and a double patty with aged cheddar and thick-cut bacon represent the burger in its most declarative, fatherly form: substantial, self-assured, not seeking anyone's approval.

My father believed in a few things absolutely: that a car should be kept clean, that a handshake should be firm, and that a burger should have two patties and enough cheese. He was not a complicated man in his appetites, and I mean that with complete admiration. Every Saturday in summer we grilled in the backyard and the burgers were always double patties with cheddar and bacon, and there was always iceberg lettuce and a specific brand of special sauce that came from a squirt bottle that he guarded with a seriousness he did not extend to the lawn or the gutters. I have made many more complicated burgers in my life than the one he made every Saturday, but none of them has ever been more correct. This burger is my attempt to honor that specific certainty — the double patty dad burger, elevated but not apologetic, with aged cheddar and thick-cut bacon and special sauce and iceberg lettuce on a brioche bun, because some things should not be changed, only understood more deeply.

Cooking a double patty to medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — is, I will acknowledge, an argument that some people push back against more than they do for a single patty. They are wrong, and the argument is worth making clearly. Two thin patties cooked to medium rare have more combined surface area browned in the Maillard reaction — more crust, more flavor, more char — than one thick patty at the same internal temperature. The interior of each patty, reaching 130 to 135 degrees, is still pink, still juicy, still carrying the gelatin and fat that make ground beef worth eating. The aged cheddar melted between the patties amplifies this — it begins to flow into the junction between the two patties, mixing with the pink juices in a way that creates a molten, savory layer of dairy and beef that is one of the genuinely transcendent experiences in burger eating. A well-done double patty is two dry discs with congealed cheese between them. A medium-rare double patty with aged cheddar is an argument for living. My father was right, and medium rare is the only way to honor what he was right about.
ingredients: 4 large eggs (3 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
6 tablespoons unsalted butter, softened and cubed
12 thick-cut slices smoked bacon (2 slices per burger)
1 tablespoon brown sugar (optional, for a slight glaze)
2 lbs ground beef (80/20 chuck) — enough for 12 thin patties (2 per burger)
12 slices aged yellow cheddar (2 per burger, about 1 oz each)
1 small head iceberg lettuce, outer leaves removed, inner leaves separated into 6 large cups
1/2 small white onion, very thinly sliced and soaked in cold water 15 minutes
Dill pickle slices (3 to 4 per burger)
instructions: 1. MAKE THE BRIOCHE BUNS — DAY BEFORE: Combine warm milk, warm water, yeast, and 1 teaspoon of the sugar in a stand mixer bowl. Let stand 5 to 8 minutes until foamy.

2. Add flour, remaining sugar, salt, and 3 eggs. Mix on low with the dough hook 2 minutes. Increase to medium 6 minutes. Add butter one cube at a time on medium speed over 8 to 10 minutes. Increase to medium-high and mix 6 to 8 minutes until smooth and elastic.
3. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover tightly with plastic wrap, and refrigerate overnight (8 to 12 hours).

4. Next day, divide dough into 6 equal portions (about 110g each). Shape each into a tight round ball. Place on parchment-lined baking sheet, spacing 3 inches apart. Cover loosely and proof 2 to 3 hours at room temperature until noticeably puffed.

5. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush buns gently with egg wash (remaining egg beaten with 1 tablespoon water). Sprinkle with sesame seeds. Bake 16 to 18 minutes until deep golden brown. Cool completely on a wire rack before slicing.

6. MAKE THE SPECIAL SAUCE: Combine mayonnaise, pickle relish, mustard, ketchup, white wine vinegar, paprika, garlic powder, onion powder, sugar, salt, and cayenne in a bowl. Stir until completely smooth. Taste and adjust sweetness, acid, and seasoning. Cover and refrigerate at least 30 minutes. The sauce improves significantly after a few hours. Keeps refrigerated for 1 week.

7. COOK THE BACON: Preheat oven to 400°F (205°C). Lay bacon slices in a single layer on a wire rack set over a rimmed baking sheet. Season with black pepper. If using, sprinkle lightly with brown sugar. Bake 15 to 18 minutes until deeply browned and very crisp. Transfer to a paper-towel-lined plate. The bacon should be completely crispy — it will hold its crunch in the assembled burger much better than pan-fried bacon. Set aside.

8. FORM THE THIN DOUBLE PATTIES: Gently combine ground chuck and ground short rib in a large bowl. Season with salt, pepper, and garlic powder and fold in gently. Divide into 12 equal portions (about 4 oz each — two thin patties per burger). Form each portion into a round patty approximately 4 1/2 inches wide and just under 1/2 inch thick. These are deliberately thin so that two of them together equal a proper double patty. Press a very shallow dimple in the center of each. Place on parchment-lined trays. Refrigerate 20 minutes.

9. COOK THE DOUBLE PATTIES: Heat a cast-iron skillet or heavy griddle over high heat until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Season the cold patties with a pinch of salt and pepper on both sides just before cooking.

10. Cook the first set of patties (the bottom patties) without pressing, 2 to 2 1/2 minutes on the first side until a deep brown crust forms. Flip once. Lay a slice of aged cheddar on each patty. Cook 1 1/2 minutes more. Check internal temperature — target 120°F (49°C) at this stage (the double-stack will reach medium rare in the next step).

11. Stack a second raw patty directly on top of the cheese-topped patty in the pan. Press down gently once to adhere. Cook the assembled double stack 1 1/2 minutes more, then flip the entire double stack. Lay a second slice of aged cheddar on top. Cook 1 1/2 to 2 minutes more. Check the internal temperature of the bottom patty — target 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium rare across the stack. Transfer to a wire rack and rest 3 minutes.
12. TOAST THE BUNS: Split brioche buns and toast cut-side down in a hot dry skillet 60 to 90 seconds until golden and crisp.
13. ASSEMBLE — BOTTOM TO TOP: Spread special sauce generously on both cut sides of the bun.
14. Place a large iceberg lettuce cup on the bottom bun — the cup shape cradles the toppings. Add 2 tomato slices and a small amount of drained white onion over the lettuce.
15. Set the rested double patty stack, cheese-side up, on the vegetables. The melted cheese should be running slightly over the edges of the patties — this is correct and good.
16. Place 3 to 4 dill pickle slices on top of the cheese. Lay the 2 bacon slices over the pickles, crossing them for full coverage.
17. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt on the bacon. Close with the top bun. Press gently once. Serve immediately.
